constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

I have to be on guard all the time

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost Community and culture' is not impossible for a combat trauma survivor, but for a 49-year-old married male European city council member it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile and is weakly anchored to the rest of the selected nodes. The rest of the profile centers on bodily danger, touch/startle, fragmented trauma recall, and safety distrust; this item instead implies a culturally/community dislocation theme that is not supported elsewhere in Triggers/Threat/Memory/Maladaptive Strategies.

issues.item: Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
issues.explanation: 'Overwhelming grief on recall' is not inherently inconsistent, but here it is the least coherent memory item relative to the formulation and other selected items. The profile is dominated by fear-based threat, bodily vulnerability, touch alarm, and cognitive disorganization of recall. A grief-dominant recall item without corresponding loss/bereavement appraisals or related strategies makes the memory cluster less internally aligned.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The profile is largely coherent for a middle-aged male combat survivor, but this appraisal is the main mismatch. 'My body has been permanently damaged' implies a salient lasting physical injury. That idea is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile: memory items focus on fragmented, terror-laden recall; threat items emphasize current danger, mistrust of safety, startle to touch, and sleep disturbance; maladaptive strategies emphasize sensory distraction, thought monitoring, and avoidance of touch. There are no triggers selected, and no other items indicate ongoing medical consequences or trauma themes centered on bodily injury. In this profile, the appraisal reads as if it belongs to a different subtype centered on physical injury rather than the represented combat-related fear/terror formulation.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile in a 49-year-old male, this specific self-blame item is the main coherence problem. The rest of the profile centers on persistent danger, touch-triggered alarm, fragmented/terror-laden memory, and defensive avoidance, which fits combat-related PTSD. In contrast, 'the event happened because of the way I acted' implies a strong internal-causal guilt formulation that is not otherwise supported by the selected memory, threat, or strategy items. This makes the appraisal set less coherent with the overall profile and with the formulation, where Memory and Threat strongly feed Negative Appraisals focused on ongoing danger rather than responsibility for causing the trauma. Self-blame can occur in combat PTSD, but here it is insufficiently connected to the other selected items and stands out as the least clinically coherent item.

vignette: As a seasoned City Council Member, John had grown accustomed to the hustle and bustle of city politics. However, beneath his composed exterior lay a complex web of emotions and memories that still lingered from his combat days. The trauma he experienced during his time in service continued to cast a long shadow over his life. It was as if his body had become an enemy, perpetually on high alert, responding to even the slightest stimuli with exaggerated startle responses. A gentle touch from his wife could send him recoiling, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios. "I just can't shake off the feeling that I'm still in danger," John would confide in her, despite her repeated assurances of safety. This deep-seated conviction had become a self-fulfilling prophecy, making it impossible for him to fully trust anyone or anything. As he navigated his daily routine, John found himself constantly monitoring his thoughts, searching for signs that he might be "losing it." He'd become adept at suppressing memories of the traumatic event, but the fragments that did surface were fragmented and disjointed. When attempting to recount what happened, John would falter, unable to articulate the sequence of events or explain the unrelenting terror that gripped him during those moments. These incomplete recollections only served to heighten his hypervigilance, as if he was perpetually poised on the precipice, waiting for disaster to strike. The world had become a perilous place in John's eyes, and he felt an overwhelming need to be constantly "on guard." His body would respond accordingly, jerking him awake in the dead of night or rendering him listless during the day. John's attempts to cope with these feelings only seemed to exacerbate them. He'd resort to loud music or TV as a sensory distraction, trying to drown out the cacophony of thoughts and emotions that threatened to consume him. However, this strategy ultimately proved counterproductive, leaving him feeling isolated and disconnected from his surroundings. In an effort to break free from this vicious cycle, John turned to avoidance behaviors, steering clear of social engagements or events that might trigger memories of the traumatic event. As a City Council Member, he found it increasingly difficult to attend meetings or interact with constituents without experiencing debilitating anxiety. His marriage began to suffer as well, his wife growing frustrated with his withdrawal from family life. John's struggles had become too much to bear alone, and he finally sought help, hoping to find a way to quiet the constant din of memories and emotions that plagued him. He longed for a sense of safety, for the ability to trust his own body and mind once more. As he embarked on this journey toward healing, John held onto the hope that he might one day be able to confront the fragmented pieces of his past, allowing himself to rebuild a life where fear was no longer the dominant narrative.
